title: Honor and shame
seoTitle: Honor and Shame in the Bible's World: What It Was Really Like
description: A long, sourced portrait of the values the Bible's first readers lived by: honor as a public verdict, challenge and envy, kin before self, gift and gratitude, the table and the guest, men and women in public, shame and vindication in Israel's Scriptures, and the cross that turned the scale over.
line: What a good name was worth, how it was won and lost, and what the gospel did to the scale, with the evidence named as we go and the arguments over it stated plainly.
intro: This is a portrait of the values the people of the Bible lived by: honor and shame, the family name, the contest in the open street, the gift and the debt of thanks, the guest at the table, the envious eye, the place of men and women in public, and the cross that turned the whole scale over. The portraits of Jewish life in Jesus's day and of the Roman world on this site already show the house, the patron and the dinner. This one goes underneath them to the values that made those things matter so much to the people who lived them.

Some of the evidence is ancient and plain. Aristotle, Seneca, Plutarch, Philo, Ben Sira and Josephus wrote about honor, gifts and gratitude in their own words, and cities carved their thanks to benefactors in stone. But the frame most readers meet today comes from modern anthropology. Studies of village life around the Mediterranean in the 1950s and 1960s, gathered in J. G. Peristiany's volume Honour and Shame (1965), were applied to the New Testament by Bruce Malina in The New Testament World (1981), and then by Jerome Neyrey, John Elliott and others in the Context Group, a working group of biblical scholars that took shape in the late 1980s. David deSilva made the approach widely readable in Honor, Patronage, Kinship and Purity (2000).

That frame has serious critics, and the page names them where they matter. Among anthropologists, Michael Herzfeld argued in 1980 that the words honor and shame glossed over many different local ideas, and others doubted the Mediterranean was one culture at all. In biblical studies, F. Gerald Downing (1999) showed that honor in one's own community was not always the first concern of ancient writers, Louise Lawrence (2003) judged the models too rigid, and Zeba Crook (2009) kept the model but corrected it. Two more cautions hold for every part. No culture runs only on shame while another runs only on guilt: the contrast goes back to Ruth Benedict's study of Japan (1946) and E. R. Dodds's use of it for early Greece (1951), and both allowed for mixtures. And nothing here describes any living people. Where a modern village custom is mentioned, such as those Kenneth Bailey reported from long years in the Middle East, it is marked as a modern parallel, not ancient evidence.

parts.title: A public verdict
parts.line: Honor was the worth other people granted you, and it belonged to a family as much as to a person.
body: In the world of the Bible, honor was not first a feeling inside a person. It was a judgment made outside, by the people whose opinion counted, about what a person and a family were worth. Bruce Malina's working definition has two halves: the worth a person claims, and the group's acknowledgment of that claim. If the town granted the claim, you had honor. If it refused, you did not, whatever you thought of yourself. Zeba Crook, revising Malina in the Journal of Biblical Literature (2009), put the point more sharply still: the public court of reputation had the power to define honor and shame as it pleased.

Ancient writers said as much in their own words. Aristotle called honor the greatest of the external goods (Nicomachean Ethics 4.3, 1123b). The usual Hebrew word for glory and honor, kavod, comes from a root that means heavy. A person of honor carried weight. When the psalmist asks, "How long, O men, will my honor be maligned?" (Psalm 4:2), that is the word he uses, and the complaint is about his name in other people's mouths.

Some honor came with birth. Anthropologists call it ascribed honor (Crook suggested attributed honor as the better term): the worth of your family, your town and your people, given before you had done anything. The rest was acquired, won through generosity, courage, skill, office and the small contests of daily life. Because birth mattered, a family tree was an honor document. Josephus opens the account of his own life with his pedigree, priestly on his father's side and descended from the Hasmonean kings on his mother's, and says he set it down as he found it in the public records (Life 1 to 6). Paul gives his own list to the Philippians: "circumcised on the eighth day, of the people of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin; a Hebrew of Hebrews; as to the law, a Pharisee" (Philippians 3:5). Then he does something no honor list was meant to do. He calls it loss.

Matthew's Gospel opens the same way: "the record of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham" (Matthew 1:1). Jerome Neyrey, in Honor and Shame in the Gospel of Matthew (1998), read the whole Gospel as an encomium, the ancient speech of praise that began with a person's birth and ancestry and went on to his deeds. Yet this list of the highest honor names four women whose stories a rival could have used against it: Tamar, Rahab, Ruth the Moabite, and the one Matthew calls only "Uriah's wife" (Matthew 1:3, 5 to 6). The genealogy claims the throne of David and does not hide the scandals on the way to it.

Ascribed honor could also close a door. When Jesus taught in the synagogue at Nazareth, the people who heard him asked where he had got such wisdom, and answered their own question with his family: "Isn't this the carpenter, the son of Mary and the brother of James, Joses, Judas, and Simon?" (Mark 6:3). They knew his house, so they knew his worth, and his words did not fit it. Mark says they took offense. In a world where worth was granted by those who knew you best, the people who had watched a man grow up were the hardest court to win.

Honor also belonged to groups more than to persons. A son's disgrace fell on his father, a daughter's on her household, a disciple's on his teacher, a citizen's on his city. That is one reason the Gospels and Paul's letters speak so much of being ashamed of someone or not: to stand next to a disgraced person was to share the disgrace. Paul thanks God for Onesiphorus, who "was unashamed of my chains" (2 Timothy 1:16), and Jesus warns that whoever is ashamed of him will find the Son of Man ashamed of them (Mark 8:38).

The model helps, and it has been pressed too far. F. Gerald Downing, in "'Honor' among Exegetes" (Catholic Biblical Quarterly, 1999), argued that ancient writers did not always put honor in their own community first, and asked whether modern Westerners are really so free of the concern. Crook argued that the honor contest was not only a game between equal men; people challenged across lines of rank and between men and women. The fair reading is that honor mattered everywhere in this world without explaining everything in it, and that people argued about what was honorable. Jesus's own question takes two courts for granted: "How can you believe if you accept glory from one another, yet do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?" (John 5:44).

read.text: When the Sabbath came, He began to teach in the synagogue, and many who heard Him were astonished. “Where did this man get these ideas?” they asked. “What is this wisdom He has been given? And how can He perform such miracles? Isn’t this the carpenter, the son of Mary and the brother of James, Joses, Judas, and Simon? Aren’t His sisters here with us as well?” And they took offense at Him. Then Jesus said to them, “Only in his hometown, among his relatives, and in his own household is a prophet without honor.”
read.note: The townspeople do not dispute the wisdom or the miracles. They dispute where they could have come from, given the family they know. Mark names the brothers and sisters so the reader can feel the weight of the village's verdict, and Jesus's proverb names the court that refused him: his hometown, his relatives, his own household.

read.text: But whatever was gain to me I count as loss for the sake of Christ. More than that, I count all things as loss compared to the surpassing excellence of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord, for whom I have lost all things. I consider them rubbish, that I may gain Christ
read.note: These verses follow a list of inherited and earned honor: the right circumcision, the right tribe, the strictest party, the zeal to prove it. Paul does not say the list was false. He says he has moved it from the gain column to the loss column, and his word for it is rubbish. To readers in a Roman colony proud of its rank, that was a startling way to talk about a good name.

read.text: How can you believe if you accept glory from one another, yet do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?
read.note: Jesus names the problem in the language of honor. The word translated glory is the same word used for a person's standing. Those who live for the approval of one another's court, he says, cannot easily hear the verdict of God's. The verse takes the whole honor system seriously and refuses to let it be the final judge.

parts.title: Challenge, reply and the evil eye
parts.line: Honor was won and lost in public exchanges, and a world that thought good things were scarce feared the envious eye.
body: The French sociologist Pierre Bourdieu studied honor among the Kabyle villagers of Algeria, and his essay in Peristiany's 1965 volume described an exchange he called challenge and riposte. A man challenges another in public. The challenge is worth answering only if it comes from an equal. The other must reply, and the onlookers decide who won; to be ignored altogether was worse than losing. Malina and others then read the controversy stories of the Gospels with this pattern in mind. A study of modern Algerian villages is not ancient evidence, so the honest test is whether the Gospels show the pattern on their own. Often they do.

Take the question about taxes. Mark says the Pharisees and Herodians were sent "to catch Jesus in His words" (Mark 12:13). They open with praise: "we know that You are honest and seek favor from no one" (12:14). Then they put a question before the crowd with two losing answers. Say yes, and he sides with Rome against his people; say no, and he is a rebel. Jesus asks for a coin, asks whose image is on it, and gives his answer, "and they marveled at Him" (12:17). Luke tells the end of the scene as a public result: "they were unable to trap Him in His words before the people; and amazed at His answer, they fell silent" (Luke 20:26).

The same shape recurs. When the chief priests ask by what authority he acts, Jesus answers with a question about John the Baptist, and when they will not commit themselves he declines to answer them (Mark 11:27 to 33). When a synagogue leader scolds the crowd for coming to be healed on the Sabbath, the reproach is aimed at Jesus through them (Luke 13:14), and Luke records the verdict of the room: "all His adversaries were humiliated. And the whole crowd rejoiced" (13:17). Matthew closes a long day of such questions with the scoreboard: "from that day on no one dared to question Him any further" (Matthew 22:46).

Crook's correction matters here. The contest was not only between equal men. A Greek woman of Syrophoenician origin asks Jesus to heal her daughter, is answered with a hard saying about bread for the children and not the dogs, and replies: "even the dogs under the table eat the children's crumbs." Jesus grants her request "because of this answer" (Mark 7:28 to 29). Scholars read that exchange in more than one way, but on any reading a foreign woman spoke back in public and was honored for it.

Beneath the contests lay an assumption anthropologists call limited good. George Foster, writing in American Anthropologist in 1965 from fieldwork in a Mexican village, described peasants who saw land, wealth, health, friendship and honor as existing in fixed amounts, so that one family could rise only at another's expense. Malina applied the idea to the biblical world. It is a modern model, and it should be used as a lens, not a law. But the Bible has scenes it fits. When the women of Israel sang, "Saul has slain his thousands, and David his tens of thousands," Saul heard praise given to David as praise taken from himself: "What more can he have but the kingdom?" (1 Samuel 18:7 to 8).

Where good is scarce, envy is dangerous, and the ancient world believed envy could strike through the eye. Plutarch's Table Talk (5.7) records a dinner conversation about people said to cast the evil eye, in which one guest argues that envy, lodged in the mind, sends harm out through the eyes like poisoned darts. A floor mosaic of the second century AD from a house at Antioch, now in the Hatay Archaeology Museum, shows a great eye attacked by a raven, a dog, a scorpion, a snake and other creatures and pierced by a trident, with two Greek words that turn the curse back on the envier: kai su, "you too." John H. Elliott gathered the evidence from Mesopotamia to the early church in four volumes, Beware the Evil Eye (2015 to 2017).

The idiom runs through the Bible. In Mark's list of what comes out of the heart, the word the Berean Standard Bible translates "envy" is in Greek "an evil eye" (Mark 7:22), and the Hebrew behind the "stingy man" of Proverbs 23:6 is a man evil of eye. In the parable of the workers, the landowner's last question is, in Greek, "Is your eye evil because I am good?" which the Berean Standard Bible renders "are you envious because I am generous?" (Matthew 20:15). Paul's "Who has bewitched you?" (Galatians 3:1) uses baskaino, the ordinary verb for casting the evil eye, its only use in the New Testament; how literally he meant it is argued. Pilate himself, in Mark's telling, "knew it was out of envy that the chief priests had handed Jesus over" (Mark 15:10).

read.text: And they were unable to trap Him in His words before the people; and amazed at His answer, they fell silent.
read.note: Luke reports the outcome the way the crowd would have scored it. The trap was meant to be sprung before the people, and it failed before the people. Their silence is the point: in a public contest, the side with nothing left to say had lost.

read.text: Do I not have the right to do as I please with what is mine? Or are you envious because I am generous?’
read.note: The Greek idiom is the evil eye. The workers hired at dawn received exactly what they agreed to, yet the landowner's goodness to the latecomers feels to them like a loss of their own. In a world that thought good things were limited, that was the natural reaction. The parable asks the hearer to see generosity without counting it as theft.

read.text: For he knew it was out of envy that the chief priests had handed Jesus over.
read.note: Mark gives the motive of the chief priests in one word. Envy was counted among the most dangerous of passions, the one that could not bear another's rise. Pilate, an outsider to the contest, could see it. The Gospel lets the reader see that the cross began, among other things, as the work of a jealous eye.

parts.title: Kin before self
parts.line: A person was known by a father, a town and a people, and the church dared to call strangers brothers and sisters.
body: Names in the Gospels carry families and places with them: Simon son of Jonah, James and John the sons of Zebedee, Jesus of Nazareth, Saul of Tarsus. The first thing a stranger needed to know was whose you were. A person was placed by a father, a household, a village and a people before anything was known of his own gifts, and his first loyalties ran back along those lines. The site's guide on singular and plural "you" follows this into Paul's letters, which were written almost entirely to groups.

That is why leaving family appears in the Gospels as a real cost, not a stage of growing up. James and John "left their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired men" (Mark 1:20), walking out of the family business in front of the men it employed. Few duties weighed more than burying a father; Joseph has to ask Pharaoh's leave to do it, and does so in those words: "let me go and bury my father, and then return" (Genesis 50:5). So when a would-be disciple asks for the same leave and hears, "Follow Me, and let the dead bury their own dead" (Matthew 8:21 to 22), the saying lands as an offense against the most honored bond a son had.

Jesus did not abolish kinship. He redrew it. When his mother and brothers came to fetch him, he pointed to his disciples: "Here are My mother and My brothers. For whoever does the will of My Father in heaven is My brother and sister and mother" (Matthew 12:49 to 50). He told his followers not to be called Rabbi, because "you are all brothers," and to call no one on earth father, "for you have one Father, who is in heaven" (Matthew 23:8 to 9). He promised that those who left houses and families for his sake would receive a hundredfold, houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children, in this age, along with persecutions (Mark 10:29 to 30). The new family came with a new household, and with trouble.

Anthropologists call this fictive kinship: family language and family duties among people not related by blood. Joseph Hellerman, in When the Church Was a Family (2009), argues that the early church chose the strongest bond its world knew, the bond between brothers and sisters, the one relationship a person could not resign. The letters speak this way without strain. Hebrews says Jesus "is not ashamed to call them brothers" (Hebrews 2:11). Paul calls the church "the family of faith" (Galatians 6:10). A young pastor is told to treat older men as fathers, younger men as brothers, older women as mothers and younger women as sisters (1 Timothy 5:1 to 2).

Outsiders noticed, and not kindly. The satirist Lucian, writing soon after AD 165 about a charlatan who had spent time among the Christians, mocks them because their first lawgiver persuaded them they were all brothers once they had denied the Greek gods and worshiped "that crucified sophist" (The Passing of Peregrinus 13, in A. M. Harmon's translation). About AD 197 Tertullian, defending the Christians of North Africa, reports that pagans were angry that Christians called one another brothers, and that they said, half in scorn, how these people love one another (Apology 39, paraphrased).

The new family could set the old one at odds, and the critics said so. The philosopher Celsus, writing in the later second century and quoted by Origen in his reply, complained that wool workers, cobblers and laundry workers in private houses would get children alone and tell them not to listen to their fathers and teachers but to them (Origen, Against Celsus 3.55). Jesus had said as much would happen: "A man's enemies will be the members of his own household" (Matthew 10:36, quoting Micah 7:6). Yet the New Testament also holds the natural family to its duties. A man who "does not provide for his own, and especially his own household," is "worse than an unbeliever" (1 Timothy 5:8). The church did not dissolve the household. It set a larger family around it.

read.text: But Jesus replied, “Who is My mother, and who are My brothers?” Pointing to His disciples, He said, “Here are My mother and My brothers. For whoever does the will of My Father in heaven is My brother and sister and mother.”
read.note: His mother and brothers are standing outside, which in a household-centered world was a claim on him. Jesus does not deny them. He enlarges the circle and names the rule of entry: doing the will of the Father. In a world where you were born into your family, this family is joined by obedience.

read.text: For both the One who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are of the same family. So Jesus is not ashamed to call them brothers.
read.note: To own someone as kin in public was to share his standing, high or low. Hebrews says the Son is not ashamed to do it. The same letter later says that God "is not ashamed to be called their God" (Hebrews 11:16). The language of honor runs both ways: God claims people the world would be ashamed to claim.

read.text: Do not rebuke an older man, but appeal to him as to a father. Treat younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, and younger women as sisters, with absolute purity.
read.note: These are family duties transferred to a congregation: respect for fathers, care for mothers, the easy speech of brothers, the protected honor of sisters. For many converts, especially slaves and those cut off by their own families, the church was not like a family. It was the only family they had.

parts.title: Gift, gratitude and loyalty
parts.line: A gift bound giver and receiver together, gratitude was a public duty, and faith meant keeping faith.
body: The site's guide on patronage and grace explains how the Greek word charis covered the giver's favor, the gift and the thanks. This part goes to the values underneath. The fullest ancient discussion is Seneca's long treatise On Benefits, written by Paul's contemporary in the middle of the first century. Seneca says that the giving and returning of benefits is the practice that most of all binds human society together (1.4.2). He opens the book with the Three Graces: some, he says, read them as one who gives, one who receives and one who returns, and they dance in a ring because a benefit passes from hand to hand and comes back to the giver (1.3). Gratitude, in this picture, was not a private glow. It was the public return of honor: praise, loyalty and service, seen by all.

That is why ingratitude was so serious. Seneca lists the crimes that will always be with us, murder, tyranny, theft, adultery, sacrilege and treason, and then says the ungrateful man is worse than all of them, because almost every great crime grows from ingratitude (1.10, paraphrased). The Gospels assume the same instinct. Of ten lepers healed, one came back, a Samaritan, and fell at Jesus's feet, and Jesus asked where the other nine were: "Was no one found except this foreigner to return and give glory to God?" (Luke 17:17 to 18). The return of thanks was the thing a gift was meant to set moving.

The Gospels show benefaction working inside Jewish towns as well. The elders of Capernaum plead for a Roman centurion with the words a city might carve on a stone: "This man is worthy to have You grant this, for he loves our nation and has built our synagogue" (Luke 7:4 to 5). Jesus knew the language and turned it. "The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those in authority over them call themselves benefactors. But you shall not be like them" (Luke 22:25 to 26). Benefactor, euergetes, was a title rulers and cities used with pride. Jesus sets beside it the youngest and the servant.

Faith belonged to the same world. The Greek pistis and the Latin fides meant trust, trustworthiness and faithfulness, the bond that held relationships together, among people and between people and their gods. Teresa Morgan, in Roman Faith and Christian Faith (2015), shows how much of the Roman world ran on it and argues that the first Christians did not invent a new meaning for the word so much as turn it toward God and Christ. Her work does not shrink faith to loyalty alone: belief that something is true belongs to it too. But a first hearer of "faith" would hear a relationship, a person to rely on and to be loyal to, more than an opinion held in private.

John Barclay's Paul and the Gift (2015) gives readers a way to see what was new in Paul's grace without pretending the ancients knew nothing of generous gifts. He names six ways a gift can be thought perfect, or carried to its extreme: its size (superabundance), the giver's pure goodwill (singularity), its coming first, before the receiver has done anything (priority), its being given without regard to the receiver's worth (incongruity), its power to change the receiver (efficacy), and its expecting nothing back (non-circularity). Barclay finds every one of them in ancient talk about gifts except the last: nearly everyone assumed a gift rightly created a return. Paul, on his reading, stresses incongruity. Grace comes to the unworthy, and it still calls for a life given back.

Here Seneca and the Gospels meet and then part. Seneca wrote that if you would imitate the gods, you must give even to the ungrateful, for the sun rises on the wicked too (4.26). Jesus used the same picture: the Father "causes His sun to rise on the evil and the good" (Matthew 5:45) and "is kind to the ungrateful and wicked" (Luke 6:35). Yet Seneca's book begins by complaining that people scatter their gifts at random instead of choosing worthy receivers, and much of it is advice on giving wisely. Jesus tells his hearers to lend expecting nothing in return and to fill their tables with people who cannot repay (Luke 6:35; 14:12 to 14). Paul draws the line plainly: one might dare to die for a good man, "But God proves His love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us" (Romans 5:7 to 8).

read.text: So Jesus declared, “The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those in authority over them call themselves benefactors. But you shall not be like them. Instead, the greatest among you should be like the youngest, and the one who leads like the one who serves.
read.note: Benefactor was an honored public title, carved on statue bases and given to kings. Jesus does not call generous rulers wicked. He says their way of turning gifts into rank is not the pattern for his followers, and he makes the youngest and the servant the measure of greatness.

read.text: But love your enemies, do good to them, and lend to them, expecting nothing in return. Then your reward will be great, and you will be sons of the Most High; for He is kind to the ungrateful and wicked.
read.note: This is the line where the Gospel leaves the ordinary rules of gift and return. Lending was expected to bring repayment, and favor was expected to bring loyalty. Jesus grounds his command in God's own way of giving, to people who will not give back, and promises that those who give this way will be sons of the Most High.

read.text: “Were not all ten cleansed?” Jesus asked. “Where then are the other nine? Was no one found except this foreigner to return and give glory to God?”
read.note: The healed foreigner does what every ancient reader knew a receiver of favor should do: he comes back and gives honor in public. The nine are not said to have done anything wrong by the law; they went to the priests as told. Jesus's question shows what he was looking for: not only obedience but the return of thanks.

modern.author: Bruce J. Malina
modern.title: The New Testament World: Insights from Cultural Anthropology
